Cassiopeia


Please do not confuse me with the [[User:Casiopedia]], as they are also an MMA editor on English Wikipedia. Welcome to my user page. I create content, fight vandalism, review [[Wikipedia:Articles for creation|Articles for creation (AfC)]] and new pages submissions. I serve as a [[Wikipedia:New pages patrol/School|New pages patrol school (NPPS)]] trainer/instructor and new user mentor, and occasionally, I also do gnomish work. I have changed my username from all caps to sentence case - see [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia:Changing_username/Usurpations&type=revision&diff=946021017&oldid=946015644&diffmode=source here] on March 18, 2020. I have a mild condition called Irlen Syndrome - see [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FARizLljRkc HERE - (at 3:19 - Washout)] so I don't see texts like normal people. Feel free to correct the grammatical mistakes in the edits I have made.

Please note that the subject failed [[WP:GNG]] and [[WP:NMMA]] notability criteria. For a subject to warrant a page in the main space of Wikipedia, it must fulfill the criteria outlined in the Wikipedia guideline on notability, specifically the General Notability Guideline (WP:GNG). GNG is defined as the subject must fulfill specific criteria to demonstrate [[WP:SIGCOV|significant coverage]] from [[WP:IS|independent]] and [[WP:RS|reliable]] sources. These sources should provide in-depth discussions about the subject rather than merely offering passing mentions. This requirement is essential for verification, which is a core policy of Wikipedia. If a source is affiliated/associated/connected with the subject—such as the subject's marketing team, company, social media platforms, information in interviews of the subject or any self-published information—this indicates a lack of independence. Consequently, such sources cannot be utilized to satisfy the notability guidelines. Sources originating from educational institutions, government entities, foundations, social media platforms, and private companies are regarded as unreliable. In contrast, materials published by "major" newspapers and "reputable" books are typically considered reliable sources. Fight announcements, fight results and fight records are all considered routine sport report and can NOT be used to meet/contribute to the notability guidelines needed. ::{U|GoldRomean}} Edit warring is not always easy to find. There are a few ways to find instances of edit warring. It is important to note that in edit warring, it's often required that "another counter-vandalism editor involvment." This is crucial so that you do not revert a page more than three times within a 24-hour period; doing so means you are involved in edit warring and risk being blocked. You can place an "edit warring template" on a user's talk page after their third disruptive revert. If they proceed with a fourth edit warring edit, then you can report them. (1) You can identify edit warring while patrolling vandalism edits. If the edits are not obvious vandalism but rather disruptive or unsourced, and (2) you need to "watch the pages" where you suspect editors might engage in edit warring, such as pages related to ongoing or upcoming special events. For example, during UFC events, if a fighter does something controversial, says something offensive or amusing, you might see a lot of vandalism and edit warring on the UFC event page or the fighter's personal page. This also applies to pages concerning recent events involving celebrities, politicians, etc. Lastly, edit warring can also occur between editors on articles about conflicts between two nations. :{{U|GoldRomean}} In English Wikipedia, the counter-vandalism warning system is flexible and differs from that of other sister sites, such as the German Wikipedia, which allows only two warnings before blocking an editor for a third act of vandalism. In English Wikipedia, we can skip warning levels based on the severity of the vandalism edits made by the editor. See examples below: :(1) If an editor is making numerous widespread and blatant vandalism edits (and not other forms of violations) within a short timeframe, and no warnings have been issued, we can issue a 4im. If the editor makes another edit after receiving the warning, we can report the editor to AIV. :(2) Suppose an editor makes a sexually explicit edit, such as referring to someone as in a derogatory context, or makes statements about engaging in inappropriate sexual activities, threatening to kill, sue, or physically harm another editor. In that case, we can issue a level 3- or 4 warning. If a subsequent edit of the same nature occurs, we can report the editor to AVI. (Note: In Wikipedia , if the gender of the editor is unknown, we use plural pronouns instead of or he or she) :(3) If an editor claims that a subject such as a politician, celebrity, or athlete is gay—despite the fact that they are married and there are no independent, reliable sources to support this assertion, we can issue a level 2 or 3 warning on the first edit. If the editor continues to make similar edits after receiving the warning, we can escalate the warning to level 4. After the third instance of such edits, we may report the editor to the appropriate authorities. :There are many instances where counter-vandalism editors can bypass the appropriate warning levels, which is determined by the assessment and decision of the counter-vandalism editor. However, it is important to provide the correct level of warnings for typical vandalism edits before reporting to AIV, as some administrators may consider the warnings insufficient and may not issue a block. You will learn to identify the appropriate warning level after completing many (thousands) of counter-vandalism edits. I hope this helps.[[User:Cassiopeia| Cassiopeia]] [[User talk:Cassiopeia|'''talk''']] 23:29, 26 May 2025 (UTC)

== PAID Editor/COI editor == Hi Paulgibbons, since you are a paid editor, please read the Wikipedia guidelines [[WP:PAID]] and [[WP:COI]]. You also need t disclose your PAID and COI on your user page and the article talk page - see [[WP:DISCLOSE]]. When you write an article, you need to write it in the draft space - see [[WP:Drafts]].
In order for a subject to warrant a page in the main space of Wikipedia, it must fulfill the criteria outlined in the Wikipedia guideline on notability, specifically the General Notability Guideline (WP:GNG). GNG is defined as the subject must fulfill specific criteria to demonstrate [[WP:SIGCOV|significant coverage]] from [[WP:IS|independent]] and [[WP:RS|reliable]] sources. These sources should provide in-depth discussions about the subject rather than merely offering passing mentions. This requirement is essential for verification, which is a core policy of Wikipedia. If a source is affiliated/associated/connected with the subject—such as the subject's marketing team, company, social media platforms, information in interviews of the subject or any self-published information—this indicates a lack of independence. Consequently, such sources cannot be utilized to satisfy the notability guidelines. Sources originating from educational institutions, government entities, foundations, social media platforms, and private companies are regarded as unreliable. In contrast, materials published by "major" newspapers and "reputable" books are typically considered reliable sources.
I recommend that you read [[WP:Your first article]] and adhere to the provided instructions before beginning the creation of an article. [[User:Cassiopeia| Cassiopeia]] [[User talk:Cassiopeia|'''talk''']] 02:23, 27 July 2025 (UTC)

The feature will be rolled out to the following Wikipedias: Azerbaijani Wikipedia, Latin Wikipedia, Macedonian Wikipedia, Malayalam Wikipedia, Marathi Wikipedia, Norwegian Nynorsk Wikipedia, Punjabi Wikipedia, Swahili Wikipedia, Telugu Wikipedia, Tagalog Wikipedia. Share your thoughts about the project. [2] Later this week, the Editing team will release Multi Check to all Wikipedias (except English Wikipedia). This feature shows multiple Reference checks within the editing experience. This encourages users to add citations when they add multiple new paragraphs to a Wikipedia article. This feature was previously available as an A/B test. The test shows that users who are shown multiple checks are 1.3 times more likely to add a reference to their edit, and their edit is less likely to be reverted (-34.7%). :{{U|Redstonedeciever}} Good day. In order for a subject to warrant a page in the main space of Wikipedia, it must fulfill the criteria outlined in the Wikipedia guideline on notability, specifically the General Notability Guideline (WP:GNG). :GNG is defined as the subject must fulfill specific criteria to demonstrate [[WP:SIGCOV|significant coverage]] from [[WP:IS|independent]] and [[WP:RS|reliable]] sources. These sources should provide in-depth discussions about the subject rather than merely offering passing mentions. This requirement is essential for verification, which is a core policy of Wikipedia. If a source is affiliated/associated/connected with the subject—such as the subject's marketing team, company, social media platforms, information in interviews of the subject or any self-published information—this indicates a lack of independence. If the new match up has not been shown in the UFC.com fight card, then we will removed the match up from the fight card and place it back to "Announced section". If the match up already shown in the UFC.com then jut put the replacement fighter in the fight card section. # When the event named has been announced (such as [[UFC Fight Night: dos Santos vs. Tuivasa]]) then we place the info in the background section (with inline citation). If UFC.com has shown the event names (Fight Night events or UFC on ESPN) such as [[UFC Fight Night: Cowboy vs. Medeiros]] or [[UFC on ESPN: Reyes vs. Weidman]], then editor would move the article and article talk page name accordingly and not before, except the flagship event such as [[UFC 187]], [[UFC 242]] and etc. # No colour box in the fighter's page infobox at event fight card page. No (c) - champion on the event fight card unless the fighter is the current champion of the weight division. #"method" in the fight table is as per Sherdog.com as per [[WP:MMA]] guideline and please do not interpret the method yourself even if the method is incorrect as Wikipedia is all about [[WP:verification]] and not the [[Wikipedia:But it's true!|true]]. #Info box as per Sherdog. [[File:HelpPage IconPack-05.png|51px|alt=|link=]]Tips
* [[Wikipedia:Be bold|Don't be afraid to edit!]] Just find something that can be improved and make it better. Other editors will help fix any mistakes you make. * It's normal to feel a little overwhelmed, but don't worry if you don't understand everything at first—it's fine to edit using common sense. * If an edit you make is reverted, you can [[Wikipedia:BOLD, revert, discuss cycle|discuss the issue at the article's talk page]]. Be civil, and don't restore the edit unless there is [[Wikipedia:Consensus|consensus]]. * Always use [[Help:Edit summary|edit summaries]] to explain your changes. * When adding new content to an article, always include a citation to a [[Help:Referencing_for_beginners#Reliable sources|reliable source]]. * If you wish to edit about a subject with which you are affiliated, read our [[Wikipedia:Plain and simple conflict of interest guide|conflict of interest guide]] and disclose your connection. * Have fun! Your presence in the Wikipedia community is welcome.

(''To request such a release, see [[Wikipedia:Requesting copyright permission]]''.) While we appreciate your contributions to Wikipedia, there are certain things you must keep in mind about using information from sources to avoid [[copyright]] and [[plagiarism]] issues. *You can only copy/translate a ''small'' amount of a source, and you must mark what you take as a direct quotation with double [[quotation mark]]s (") and cite the source using an [[Wikipedia:Inline citation|inline citation]]. You can read about this at [[Wikipedia:Non-free content]] in the sections on "text". See also [[Help:Referencing for beginners]], for how to cite sources here.{{#ifeq: | 1 |}} *Aside from limited quotation, you must put all information ''in your own words and structure'', in proper [[paraphrase]]. Following the source's words too closely can create [[derivative work|copyright problems]], so it is not permitted here; see [[Wikipedia:Close paraphrasing]]. Even when using your own words, you are still, however, asked to cite your sources to [[Wikipedia:Verifiability|verify]] the information and to demonstrate that the content is not [[Wikipedia:No original research|original research]].{{#ifeq: | 2 |}} *We have strict guidelines on the usage of copyrighted images. [[Fair use]] images must meet all ten of the [[Wikipedia:Non-free content criteria|non-free content criteria]] in order to be used in articles, or they will be deleted. Understand, though, that unlike many other sites, where a person can license their content for use there and retain non-free ownership, that is not possible at Wikipedia. Rather, the release of content must be irrevocable, ''to the world'', into either the [[public domain]] (PD) or under a [[Wikipedia:FAQ/Copyright#Can I add something to Wikipedia that I got from somewhere else?|suitably free and compatible]] copyright license. If you want to copy or translate from another Wikipedia project or article, you must follow the copyright attribution steps described at [[Wikipedia:Copying within Wikipedia]]. See also [[Help:Translation#License requirements]]. ==Etymology== The word ''ōtsuchi'' derives from two Japanese elements: ''ō'' (大), meaning "large" or "great," and ''tsuchi'' (槌), meaning "hammer" or "mallet."<ref>Nakamura, K. ''Japanese-English Dictionary of Military Terminology''. Kodansha, 1977, p. 241.</ref> Together, the term literally translates to "large hammer." This distinguishes it from smaller hammers (tsuchi) used in carpentry or ritual contexts. The sheer size and weight required both hands for effective use. Similarly, in European contexts, it resembles the medieval battering ram or war hammer, though adapted for Japanese material culture. * Video games such as role-playing or fighting games sometimes include oversized hammers as weapon options, indirectly referencing the ōtsuchi. * Festivals and historical reenactments sometimes feature replicas of the ōtsuchi, highlighting its place in Japanese martial heritage.

Ōtsuchi.added_text: (183 The '''ōtsuchi''' (大槌, "large hammer" or "war mallet") is a traditional Japanese two-handed war mallet used primarily during the [[feudal Japan|feudal era]]. Unlike bladed weapons such as the [[katana]] or polearms such as the [[naginata]], the ōtsuchi was a blunt-force instrument, resembling an oversized wooden mallet or sledgehammer. Typically constructed of heavy wood, sometimes reinforced with iron, the ōtsuchi was not commonly used for direct combat but for breaching doors, gates, or fortifications. Its design and purpose align it with siege implements rather than battlefield sidearms, yet it occupies a place in the corpus of Japanese martial weaponry.<ref>Bottomley, Ian, and Anthony Hopson. ''Arms and Armor of the Samurai: The History of Weaponry in Ancient Japan''. Crescent Books, 1990, p. 142.</ref> ==Etymology== The word ''ōtsuchi'' derives from two Japanese elements: ''ō'' (大), meaning "large" or "great," and ''tsuchi'' (槌), meaning "hammer" or "mallet."<ref>Nakamura, K. ''Japanese-English Dictionary of Military Terminology''. Kodansha, 1977, p. 241.</ref> Together, the term literally translates to "large hammer." This distinguishes it from smaller hammers (tsuchi) used in carpentry or ritual contexts. ==Historical context== During the [[Heian period]] (794–1185), most warfare in Japan emphasized mounted archery and swords. However, as castles and fortified structures developed during the Kamakura (1185–1333) and Muromachi periods (1336–1573), siege warfare became increasingly important.<ref>Turnbull, Stephen. ''Samurai Siege Warfare: The Rise of the Japanese Castle''. Osprey Publishing, 2002, pp. 45–50.</ref> The ōtsuchi emerged in this context as a practical tool for breaking gates, doors, and barricades. Its blunt force could shatter wooden barriers that would resist bladed or piercing weapons. Though not as iconic as swords or spears, the ōtsuchi held tactical significance. Samurai and ashigaru (foot soldiers) carrying the mallet typically accompanied assault units in castle sieges, where speed in breaching an entryway could determine victory or defeat.<ref>Yumoto, John M. ''The Samurai Sword: A Handbook''. Tuttle Publishing, 1958, p. 88.</ref> ==Design and construction== The ōtsuchi generally measured around six feet (1.8 meters) in length, comparable to a long staff weapon.<ref>Friday, Karl F. ''Samurai, Warfare and the State in Early Medieval Japan''. Routledge, 2004, p. 134.</ref> The head was a massive wooden block, cylindrical or rectangular in shape, secured to a wooden shaft. While many were entirely of hardwood, some extant examples and descriptions suggest reinforcement with iron bands to increase durability and impact power.<ref>Sinclair, David A. ''Weapons of the Samurai''. Chartwell Books, 2013, p. 73.</ref> The sheer size and weight required both hands for effective use. This limited mobility in open combat but made the weapon devastating against immobile targets. In training, ōtsuchi-like tools may have been used to build strength, as their weight demanded considerable endurance. ==Usage== ===Siege warfare=== The primary function of the ōtsuchi was in siege warfare. Samurai chronicles occasionally mention the use of heavy hammers in castle assaults. A coordinated group could swing the mallet repeatedly against doors until they collapsed.<ref>Turnbull, Stephen. ''Samurai Castles 1540–1640''. Osprey Publishing, 2003, pp. 61–63.</ref> This was often performed under cover from archers or shield bearers, as the attackers were vulnerable while striking the gate. ===Ritual and symbolic use=== Beyond combat, the ōtsuchi has symbolic resonance in Japanese folklore. The ''uchide no kozuchi'' (打ち出の小槌), or "magic mallet," appears in tales such as that of the [[Issun-bōshi]], where a miniature hero wields a mallet granting wishes.<ref>Seki, Keigo. ''Folktales of Japan''. University of Chicago Press, 1963, p. 211.</ref> Though distinct from the war mallet, the association illustrates how hammers, both real and mythical, carried cultural meaning. === Martial arts training === While no classical koryū (old martial arts schools) treat the ōtsuchi as a primary battlefield weapon, training with heavy wooden implements was sometimes used to develop strength. Comparable to suburitō (heavy wooden swords), the mallet served as conditioning equipment.<ref>Friday, Karl. ''Legacies of the Sword: The Kashima-Shinryu and Samurai Martial Culture''. University of Hawaii Press, 1997, p. 102.</ref> ==Cultural significance== Although not as romanticized as the katana, the ōtsuchi embodies the practical aspect of Japanese warfare. Its presence in siege contexts emphasizes the importance of combined arms: swordsmen, archers, engineers, and breachers working in tandem.<ref>Turnbull, Stephen. ''The Samurai Sourcebook''. Cassell & Co., 1998, p. 228.</ref> In art and popular culture, the mallet appears less frequently than other weapons. However, its mythical cousin, the magic mallet, is common in [[ukiyo-e]] prints and children's tales. Modern manga, anime, and games sometimes depict characters wielding oversized hammers reminiscent of the ōtsuchi, exaggerating its scale for comedic or dramatic effect. ==Comparison with similar weapons== The ōtsuchi is sometimes compared to the [[kanabō]], a spiked or studded club also used by samurai. While both are blunt-force weapons, the kanabō was designed for direct combat, whereas the ōtsuchi functioned primarily as a breaching tool.<ref>Sinclair, David A. ''Weapons of the Samurai''. Chartwell Books, 2013, p. 74.</ref> Similarly, in European contexts, it resembles the medieval battering ram or war hammer, though adapted for Japanese material culture. ==Modern depictions== In modern popular culture, the ōtsuchi is occasionally reimagined: * In manga and anime, large hammers are often wielded by female characters for comedic effect, inspired by the exaggerated size of the traditional mallet.<ref>Napier, Susan J. ''Anime from Akira to Howl’s Moving Castle: Experiencing Contemporary Japanese Animation''. Palgrave, 2005, p. 188.</ref> * Video games such as role-playing or fighting games sometimes include oversized hammers as weapon options, indirectly referencing the ōtsuchi. * Festivals and historical reenactments sometimes feature replicas of the ōtsuchi, highlighting its place in Japanese martial heritage.

Sasumata.removed_text: Their symbolic presence outside official buildings served both practical and ceremonial purposes, emphasizing the authority of the Tokugawa legal system. The fork could be used to pin a suspect’s neck, torso, or limbs against a wall or the ground. Because the long shaft allowed multiple officers to restrain a suspect simultaneously, the weapon served as a force multiplier in group arrests. The design reflected a compromise between practicality, intimidation, and the Tokugawa regime’s emphasis on order without bloodshed. *Neck restraint: The fork encircled the suspect’s neck or chest, holding them against a surface. *Limb control: Arms or legs could be trapped in the fork, preventing further movement. *Crowd control: In riots or brawls, multiple officers could use sasumata to push or contain individuals. *Symbolic presence: Displayed in front of checkpoints, the tool warned passersby of the shogunate’s readiness to enforce order. ==Cultural and Symbolic Role== Beyond their functional purpose, sasumata were status markers of Edo-period police. They appeared in processions, official illustrations, and later in kabuki theater, reinforcing their identity as instruments of justice.<ref name="Mol2003" /> Museums in Japan frequently display them as part of Edo-era police equipment, emphasizing their importance in the daily life of Tokugawa society. Despite its appeal as a non-lethal restraint device, modern sasumata use raises issues: *Effectiveness: Against determined or armed attackers, sasumata may prove insufficient. *Psychological effects: The presence of forked poles in classrooms has been criticized as potentially traumatizing for children. *Legal issues: Civilian use of force can expose users to lawsuits or criminal liability if excessive harm occurs. name="Mol2003" Although some sources place the origin of the sasumata in the [[Muromachi]] period, most sources discuss its use in the [[Edo period]]. In Edo period Japan the samurai were in charge of police operations. ===Firefighting=== There were also firefighting versions of the instrument known as a ''chokyakusan'', ''rinkaku'', ''tetsubashira'', or ''tokikama''. A similar weapon in China{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}} was known as a ''chang jiao qian'', and sometimes called a ''cha gan'' or ''huo cha'' (fire fork), which had a similar firefighting role.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}} The sasumata type implements were used by firefighters to help dismantle burning buildings, raise ladders, and otherwise assist with their duties.

Sasumata.added_text: ==Etymology== The term ''sasumata'' combines the Japanese words 刺 (sasu, "to stab" or "to thrust") and 股 (mata, "fork" or "crotch"), literally meaning "thrusting fork." The name highlights its dual nature: a polearm-like implement but primarily designed to restrain or pin a suspect against the ground or wall.<ref name="Mol2003" /> ==Historical Background== ===Early development=== Although the exact origin of the sasumata is uncertain, it is believed to have developed from agricultural tools and battlefield implements during the late Muromachi period (1336–1573). Its design was influenced by earlier polearms and anti-cavalry devices but adapted for urban policing during the peaceful Edo period.<ref name="Mol2003" /> ===Edo-period policing=== During the Tokugawa shogunate, policing responsibilities were entrusted to samurai retainers, low-ranking officials, and specialized officers. The state discouraged unnecessary bloodshed, especially in densely populated urban centers such as Edo (Tokyo), Osaka, and Kyoto. To enforce order, law enforcement relied on tools that allowed suspects to be subdued without lethal force.<ref name="Cunningham2004" /> The sasumata, *tsukubō*, and *sodegarami* became standardized equipment for police outposts (''bansho''), checkpoints, and magistrates’ offices. These tools were collectively called the ''torimono sandōgu'' and were part of a broader system of six implements known as the ''bansho rokugin'' (the "six implements of a guardhouse").<ref name="Mol2003" /> Their symbolic presence outside official buildings served both practical and ceremonial purposes, emphasizing the authority of the Tokugawa legal system. ==Description and Design== A traditional sasumata was approximately 2 meters (6.5 feet) in length, with a wooden shaft reinforced by iron fittings. The working end consisted of a large, U-shaped fork, often equipped with inward-facing barbs or spikes. These prevented suspects from grabbing the pole and added psychological deterrence.<ref name="Mol2003" /> The opposite end was capped with an ''ishizuki'' (butt cap), a metal fitting commonly found on other Japanese polearms, both for protection and balance.<ref name="Cunningham2004" /> The fork could be used to pin a suspect’s neck, torso, or limbs against a wall or the ground. Because the long shaft allowed multiple officers to restrain a suspect simultaneously, the weapon served as a force multiplier in group arrests. The design reflected a compromise between practicality, intimidation, and the Tokugawa regime’s emphasis on order without bloodshed. == Techniques of Use == ===Taiho-jutsu=== The use of the sasumata was integrated into a broader system of arresting techniques known as ''taiho-jutsu'' ("arresting arts"). Officers trained to immobilize suspects with minimal harm, then secure them using rope-tying methods from ''hojōjutsu''.<ref name="Cunningham2004" /> === Arrest scenarios === *Neck restraint: The fork encircled the suspect’s neck or chest, holding them against a surface. *Limb control: Arms or legs could be trapped in the fork, preventing further movement. *Crowd control: In riots or brawls, multiple officers could use sasumata to push or contain individuals. *Symbolic presence: Displayed in front of checkpoints, the tool warned passersby of the shogunate’s readiness to enforce order. Because Edo-period law demanded suspects be brought in alive whenever possible, the sasumata epitomized non-lethal but coercive policing.<ref name="Mol2003" /> ==Cultural and Symbolic Role== Beyond their functional purpose, sasumata were status markers of Edo-period police. They appeared in processions, official illustrations, and later in kabuki theater, reinforcing their identity as instruments of justice.<ref name="Mol2003" /> Museums in Japan frequently display them as part of Edo-era police equipment, emphasizing their importance in the daily life of Tokugawa society. ==Decline and Survival== With the Meiji Restoration (1868) and modernization of police forces along Western lines, the torimono sandōgu, including the sasumata, declined in regular law enforcement use. Firearms, batons, and handcuffs became standard. Nevertheless, the sasumata survived as a cultural artifact and training tool in some martial arts schools specializing in traditional arresting techniques.<ref name="Cunningham2004" /> ==Modern Usage== ===School security=== In the aftermath of the 2001 Ikeda Elementary School massacre in Osaka, many Japanese schools sought practical, non-lethal means of defense against intruders. Modern sasumata, typically made of aluminum and designed with padded, blunt forks, were introduced into classrooms as emergency restraint tools.<ref name="Guardian2023" /> ===Police and civilian contexts=== While not part of standard police issue nationwide, some Japanese police departments retain modern sasumata for riot control or special scenarios. Businesses, such as convenience stores and jewelry shops, also stock them for self-defense against robbers. A widely publicized 2023 incident in Tokyo involved a jewelry store employee fending off would-be robbers with a sasumata, sparking renewed interest and sales.<ref name="Guardian2023" /> === Training and challenges === Critics point out that effective use of sasumata requires training to avoid accidental harm. Without proper instruction, users may fail to immobilize suspects safely. There are also debates about liability in cases where injury occurs during civilian use.<ref name="Cunningham2004" /> ==Comparisons with Other Tools== The sasumata shares similarities with other cultural restraint devices: * The European '''man catcher''' featured a similar forked design intended to pull riders off horses or restrain suspects.<ref>[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_catcher "Man catcher"]. ''Wikipedia''.</ref> * Chinese military history includes polearms with crescent or forked heads used to control enemies at a distance. * Within Japan, the sasumata was functionally paired with the ''tsukubō'' (push pole) and ''sodegarami'' (sleeve entangler), together forming the essential set of torimono sandōgu.<ref name="Mol2003" /> ==Criticism and Concerns== Despite its appeal as a non-lethal restraint device, modern sasumata use raises issues: *Effectiveness: Against determined or armed attackers, sasumata may prove insufficient. *Psychological effects: The presence of forked poles in classrooms has been criticized as potentially traumatizing for children. *Legal issues: Civilian use of force can expose users to lawsuits or criminal liability if excessive harm occurs. *Training burden: Proper restraint techniques must be taught; otherwise, the tool could become ineffective or dangerous.<ref name="Cunningham2004" /> ==In Martial Arts== The sasumata is preserved in certain martial traditions, particularly within ''taiho-jutsu'' and ''koryū'' schools that emphasize Edo-period arresting techniques. Martial arts demonstrations often include mock scenarios of subduing an armed opponent with sasumata, showcasing both its practical heritage and symbolic role.<ref name="Mol2003" ==Legacy== Today, the sasumata represents both a fascinating artifact of Tokugawa policing and a modern example of how historical tools are repurposed for contemporary safety concerns. Its enduring presence in Japanese schools, museums, and martial arts halls underscores the continuity between past and present approaches to law enforcement and self-defense.

The bout is expected to proceed at catchweight and she will be fined a percentage of her purse, which will go to her opponent former [[Invicta Fighting Championships#Bantamweight Championship|Invicta FC Bantamweight Champion]] and [[UFC Women's Featherweight Championship]] challenger [[Yana Santos]].<ref name="weighins">{{Cite web|url=https://mmajunkie.usatoday.com/story/sports/ufc/2025/10/03/ufc-320-ankalaev-pereira-dvalishvili-sandhagen-title-weigh-in-results-live-video-stream/86481602007/|title=UFC 320 weigh-in results: One heavy in Vegas, but title fighters on point|publisher=mmajunkie.usatoday.com|author=Staff|date=2025-10-03|access-date=2025-10-03}}</ref> The featherweight bout between Daniel Santos and Yoo Joo-sang was also changed to a catchweight bout of 153 pounds.<ref name="weighins"/> === Daniel Santos weight miss === During the official weigh-ins October 3, the significantly impacted by a major weight miss from one of the fighters. Santos registered a weight of 151 pounds, a full five pounds over the 146-pound limit for non-title fights. A weight discrepancy of this magnitude is considered a serious professional infraction, as it creates a considerable physical advantage for the fighter who missed weight and places the compliant opponent at a significant disadvantage. As a direct result of the weigh-in failure, the bout was officially converted contest. In accordance with the athletic commission's regulations, Santos was penalized with a fine 30 percent of his guaranteed purse (also known as "show money"), which was awarded to his opponent, Yoo Joo-sang, as compensation. It was confirmed that this penalty applies only to the show money and not to any potential win bonus Santos could earn. Despite the challenging and unfair circumstances, Yoo Joo-sang's camp formally agreed to the new terms, allowing the bout to proceed on the card.<ref name="MMAJunkieWeighIns">{{cite news|last=Lee|first=John|title=UFC 320 weigh-in results: Daniel Santos misses weight by 5 pounds, fined 30 percent of show money|url=https://mmajunkie.usatoday.com/2025/10/ufc-320-ankalaev-pereira-weigh-in-results-live-stream|work=MMA Junkie|date=October 3, 2025|access-date=October 4, 2025}}</ref><ref name="UFC320WeighIns">{{cite web|title=UFC 320: Ankalaev vs. Pereira 2 Official Weigh-in Results|url=https://www.ufc.com/news/official-weigh-results-ufc-320-ankalaev-vs-pereira-2|website=UFC.com|date=October 3, 2025|access-date=October 4, 2025}}</ref>
